h1: West Coast IPA and New England IPA tasted side by side
title: West Coast vs New England IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: Taste a West Coast IPA and a New England IPA together and learn what to look for in colour, aroma, bitterness, body and finish.
teaser: One is clear, dry and bitter. The other is hazy, soft and juicy. Taste them together and you will never confuse them again.
standfirst: West Coast and New England IPAs both use a lot of hops, but they are built to feel completely different. A side by side tasting is the fastest way to learn why. This guide tells you exactly what to look for.
sections: Two answers to the same question

Both styles ask how much hop flavour a beer can carry. The West Coast IPA, developed by American brewers on the Pacific coast, answers with bitterness and clarity: a dry, pale, crystal clear beer with a sharp hop bite. The New England IPA, which spread from the north-east of the United States, answers with aroma and softness: a hazy, juicy beer with much less perceived bitterness.

On paper they can share hop varieties and similar strength, usually 6 to 7.5% ABV. In the glass they behave like different drinks.

Buy one fresh example of each, ideally from the same brewery so the comparison is fair. Check the packaging date. IPAs fade fast. A stale one tells you nothing about the style. Chill both to about 7 to 8 °C and pour into identical glasses, such as a tulip or a standard pint.

Taste the West Coast first. Its bitterness can linger, but starting with the softer beer and then moving to the sharp one makes the bitterness jump out unfairly. Keep water and plain crackers nearby and take notes as you go.

The West Coast IPA should be pale gold to light amber and clear enough to read through. Brewers filter or let the beer settle cold to get that brightness.

The New England IPA is opaque, from pale straw to orange, often compared to orange juice. The haze comes from proteins in oats and wheat, polyphenols from heavy dry hopping and yeast that stays in suspension. Our guide on hazy versus clear beer explains when haze is intended and when it is a fault.

Lift each glass and smell before you sip. The West Coast IPA tends toward pine, resin, grapefruit pith and sometimes a dank, herbal note. You may catch a light biscuit malt underneath.

The New England IPA leans tropical and ripe: mango, passion fruit, peach, pineapple and orange. Much of this comes from hops added late or during fermentation, where yeast can transform hop compounds into fruitier forms. If you have eaten a ripe Alphonso mango, you may recognise some of it.

Now sip. This is where the difference is clearest.

  • Bitterness. The West Coast IPA has firm, lasting bitterness, often 50 to 70 IBU. It hits early. The New England IPA may measure 30 to 50 IBU but feels softer still, because its fuller body and higher residual sweetness blunt the bitterness.
  • Body. The West Coast is light and crisp. The New England feels round, smooth and almost creamy, thanks to oats, wheat and water with more chloride than sulphate.
  • Sweetness. West Coast IPAs ferment very dry. New England IPAs finish a little sweeter.

Pay attention to where the flavour sits on your tongue and how long it lasts after you swallow.
Finish: dry snap or soft fade

The West Coast IPA finishes dry and bitter, with resin hanging on. It invites another sip because it leaves your mouth clean. The New England IPA fades softly, with fruit lingering and a slight sweetness. Some people find a gentle hop burn on the throat from the heavy dry hopping. That is a common feature, though too much of it is a flaw.

Write a single sentence for each beer. If you can describe them without using the words bitter and juicy, you are tasting well.
What to pair and when to choose

The West Coast IPA is the better partner for rich, fried or fatty food. Its bitterness and carbonation cut through pakoras, fried fish and butter-heavy dishes. The New England IPA works with spicier, fruitier dishes where its sweetness can calm the heat, such as a Goan prawn curry or a spicy chaat.

In Indian conditions, freshness matters even more for the hazy style. Its fruity aromas fade within weeks if the beer sits warm. The haze can turn muddy and taste of cardboard. Buy it from a cold shelf, drink it soon and do not age it.

One tasting gives you the basics. Describing differences precisely across many beers is a trained skill, built through practice with reference samples and a shared vocabulary.
faqs: Why are New England IPAs hazy?
The haze comes from proteins in oats and wheat, polyphenols from heavy dry hopping and yeast in suspension. Brewers intend it, so it is not a fault in this style.
The West Coast IPA. It is brewed for firm, lasting bitterness and a dry finish, while the New England IPA is designed to taste soft and fruity.
Do New England IPAs go stale faster?
Usually yes. Their delicate fruit aromas and hop-derived haze break down quickly, especially in warm storage. Drink them fresh and keep them cold.
What temperature should I serve IPAs at?
Around 7 to 10 °C. Colder hides the hop aroma, while warmer can make the bitterness and alcohol stand out.
